source.title: SAFE: Finding Sparse and Flat Minima to Improve Pruning
source.authors: Dongyeop Lee; Kwanhee Lee; J. Chung; Namhoon Lee

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some table and figure layouts are flattened, but the relevant numeric comparisons are recoverable from the stated tables and text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures flatness and reports generalization-related outcomes for sparse networks, using a pruning and sharpness-aware training method rather than directly testing the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation accuracy, perplexity, sharpness, and robustness outcomes for its own pruning method and comparator pruning methods. These results bear on V7's measured flatness/generalization relationship in part, but do not test the stated magnitude-aware perturbation measure or rank it against norm- and margin-based measures. Results that only compare pruning performance across methods are not rows for V1–V6 or V8.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization premise to design and evaluate SAFE pruning. Its own results measure induced flatness, pruning accuracy, perplexity, and robustness. It does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its association with training–test gaps, and it tests none of V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that SAFE finds sparse, flat solutions, generally improves pruning performance, and improves robustness to training and inference noise; SAFE+ further improves LLM pruning. These are method-performance conclusions, not evidence for V7's specific magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship. Claims of superiority should remain qualified: SAFE does not beat every comparator in every setting.
record.recipe_differences: The study jointly trains sparse networks with a sharpness-aware objective and evaluates pruning performance; V7 concerns measuring magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its relation to generalization gaps among similarly trained networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Penalty parameter and its schedule, target sparsity, dual-update interval, and batch-norm tuning affect pruning outcomes; the reported flatness comparison is between SAFE and ADMM on a small MLP.

fits_no_version.finding: On MNIST, 3-layer MLPs with hidden widths 300 and 100 and 90% target sparsity yield maximum Hessian eigenvalues of 0.09 for SAFE and 0.2 for ADMM (Figure 1; Appendix B.2). Flatness is explicitly encouraged during SAFE training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAFE induces lower maximum Hessian eigenvalues than ADMM in this sparse-MLP experiment. This does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or a sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

fits_no_version.finding: SAFE and SAFE+ improve many pruning accuracy and perplexity comparisons, and SAFE improves robustness to partial label corruption and inference-time corruptions (Sections 4.2–4.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness-aware sparsification can improve retained predictive performance and robustness relative to selected pruning baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: At 25% label noise, ADMM validation accuracy varies nonmonotonically with pruning sparsity; the authors describe sparse double descent and report its absence with SAFE (Section 4.4; Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning sparsity can produce nonmonotonic validation performance under label noise. This does not test widening beyond an identified zero-training-error threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The flatness comparison uses a single standard 3-layer MLP on MNIST and reports a qualitative loss-landscape comparison plus maximum Hessian eigenvalues, without a quantitative training–test gap analysis. Many pruning accuracy results do not isolate flatness as the cause of the performance difference.
record.rows_left_out: No row retained: pruning accuracy and perplexity comparisons do not measure a behavior named in V1–V8. The flatness result in Figure 1 is not a measure of the magnitude-aware sharpness or gap relationship required by V7.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization using the same architecture and training recipe; chance held-out accuracy with random labels. Partial label-noise robustness experiments do not establish these comparisons.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error. Varying pruning sparsity does not establish this width-dependent relationship.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning budgets and recovery through broader tuning or modified optimization recipes.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the generalization penalty.
Controlled dropout comparisons, including training-set size, excessive dropout, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its correlation with training–test gaps among convolutional networks with similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy loss.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's relation from tests to uses_without_test and tranche from T2 to T4. Its empty result rows are appropriate for V1–V8, and the excluded results are already declared in rows_left_out. No version-level verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Generalization as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization on image tasks.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization under tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on test error and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.

Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures. The study measures maximum Hessian eigenvalue and reports a qualitative comparison with ADMM, but does not measure the version's named magnitude-aware sharpness or relate it to training–test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples versus random examples and measuring test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
